noi_dung:
Instructions for the Amitabha Session

In the Saha world, everyone loves pleasure and hates suffering. Beings in the hells love suffering and hate pleasure. Hungry ghosts love anger and hate compassion. Animals, because they loved stupidity and hated wisdom, fell into animality.

Although people love happiness and hate suffering, they do not know how to be free of suffering. In the heavens, everyone loves pleasure and hates suffering. Meanwhile, for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, their state has neither suffering nor pleasure. They have completely forgotten both states of suffering and joy. Most living beings are upside down—taking right for wrong and wrong for right, black for white and white for black. In the end, do living beings know they are upside down? They do! Yet though they know, they still do wrong; though they clearly understand a thing is irrational, they insist on doing it; though they know what is right, they refuse to do it.

For example, some people go off to drink tea right in the middle of Buddha-recitation. Drinking tea also has its set time; it cannot be done casually, anytime and anywhere. Using Buddha-recitation time to drink tea is laziness. "Reciting the Buddha is too tiring; I'll go drink a cup of tea and rest a while"—that is being lazy. If you sincerely recited the Buddha, how would you still think of drinking tea? You would long ago have completely forgotten about drinking tea, let alone drinking milk, for you must forget everything! One who truly recites the Buddha does not even know whether he has eaten, let alone drinking tea?

Someone says: "Reciting the Buddha that way is too dangerous, because it makes you forget even whether you've eaten!" Yet this is precisely the skill of those who truly apply effort—whether they have eaten or not, they do not know; whether they have dressed or not, they do not remember; whether they have rested or not, they are unaware. Forgetting everything! Daytime? Don't know! Nighttime? Don't know. Above, no sky is seen; below, no earth is seen; in between, no people are known—everything is empty. When all things are empty, how could you still remember drinking tea or drinking milk?

At Gold Mountain Monastery there is a monk who dares not drink milk. For after drinking milk, sexual desire arises and cannot be controlled; therefore he does not drink milk. We eat and drink to sustain life, taking food as medicine. Without eating we would starve, so we eat to stay alive—it is not that we need nourishing foods to pamper the body. When food is too rich, there is great trouble.

One who practices the Buddha-recitation Dharma-door must remember at all times to recite only the single phrase "Nam Mô A Di Đà Phật", without ever stopping. Recite it awake, recite it asleep. You must recite the six-syllable honored name "Nam Mô A Di Đà Phật" so that nothing can interrupt it—even a sword could not cut it off. The power of Buddha-recitation must be firm, surpassing even the hardness of vajra. When no means at all can destroy your recitation of "Nam Mô A Di Đà Phật", only then is it called "Buddha-recitation samadhi."

Not only Buddha-recitation is so, but Sutra recitation and mantra holding are the same. In that state, even if you wanted to give rise to discursive thoughts, you could not. Cultivation is no easy matter. Look at Master Heng Sure: why doesn't he drink milk? Because he knows the harm in milk! As soon as he drinks cow's milk, the "cow nature" at once flares up. And when that "cow nature" (sexual desire) flares up, it is fiercer than a tiger!

Ordinarily, if the body lacks no nutrition, there is no need for rich supplements. Eating rich foods brings all kinds of trouble. Hence, "excess is just like deficiency"—going too far and falling short are both unwholesome.

Living beings in this Saha world—every movement, every act is greed, anger, and delusion. Cultivating worldly dharmas, beings use greed, anger, and delusion to cultivate. Cultivating world-transcending dharmas, they still use greed, anger, and delusion to cultivate. Thus, as they cultivate they crave enlightenment—sitting in Chan for two and a half days and already wanting to become enlightened, practicing not yet three days and demanding spiritual powers, reciting the Buddha only a few days and demanding Buddha-recitation samadhi. Just see how enormous their greed is! These are all expressions of hungry ghosts.

We should treat cultivation as our own duty, with no need for greed—in time, merit and virtue will be perfected, and the fruit of Bodhi will naturally ripen. Cultivation would already have succeeded, but just because you are too greedy, in the end you cannot "digest" it. Like eating rice: you must chew one mouthful at a time; if you cram a whole bowl into your mouth at once, your mouth full, how can you eat? You can neither chew nor swallow. Eating is a very simple example. Hence the saying: "The greedy bite off more than they can chew."

In cultivation, you must cultivate as if cultivating nothing at all. Do not give rise to greed, nor calculate what you will become or what you will get. You want enlightenment, you want spiritual powers; but how could you attain results so quickly? When a seed is sown in the ground, you must wait for it to slowly grow tall; and when the time is full, it will ripen. The ancients taught:

"Grind an iron rod into a needle;

With enough effort, it naturally becomes."

Do not fear wasted effort; when the time is full, even iron will be ground into a needle—with effort in grinding iron, the day comes when it becomes a needle.

In cultivation, the essential point is to eradicate all bad habits and faults. What are bad habits and faults? Fondness for tea is a fault, fondness for milk is a fault, fondness for giving rise to scattered discursive thoughts is also a fault. If you crave comfort, your skill will win no sympathetic response. In applying effort, do not fear suffering, hardship, or fatigue—only then will cultivation succeed. Here I must apologize to you, for I love to joke, so those of you who are plump, after hearing my talks, please do not go on a diet to shed fat and slim down. Otherwise, I fear you will be "putting a head on top of your head"—doing useless things and creating all kinds of afflictions for yourselves.

Today, the whole world is everywhere filled with natural and man-made calamities. Everywhere has turned dark, without light, showing that humankind's very existence is gravely threatened. That murderous atmosphere is truly unprecedented. You have heard of the atomic bomb, the hydrogen bomb, nuclear weapons, and now there is the laser besides. Should such weapons ever be used, all humanity would surely perish. Thus the entire globe is now shrouded in a dark, sinister aura, and dark evil karma blankets the land. The only way to dispel such calamities is for us to rely on the Buddhadharma in our cultivation. Wherever there are people truly cultivating, there calamities will lessen. If many people join together in cultivation, the collective strength can eradicate calamities, dissolving that cruel, poisonous aura into an air of peace and auspiciousness. For this, everyone must truly practice, genuinely walking the Way according to the Buddhadharma.

Recite the Buddha with sincerity. With each recitation of the Buddha, a beam of light appears in empty space. If you sincerely and earnestly recite the Buddha, that beam of light will shine throughout the great trichiliocosm, and can dissolve all pollution, violence, and calamity, making the atmosphere of the great trichiliocosm wholesome.

The City of Ten Thousand Buddhas is a luminous place in this world, radiating light throughout the universe. If you give rise to discursive thoughts even while at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, you still earn merit—greater merit, in fact, than the greatest merit you could earn in the outside world. Why do I say this? Because everyone at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas turns toward goodness, so even their discursive thoughts are mostly good ones; rarely do they think of evil. Thus you could say the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas is the sun and moon of the world, shining everywhere and bringing all beings purity and coolness.

All who dwell at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas planted many good roots long ago. They once vowed to improve the world and dissolve all calamities. Therefore, dwelling at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, you must walk the proper path in cultivation—in every act and every word. Do not follow along with bad or vulgar people. Those who live at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas are all good, upstanding people. Those with fierce temperaments and evil minds, sooner or later, will be unable to stay and will leave the monastery of their own accord.

The City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, rising from the earth in the West, is where Buddhists of the whole world will gather in the future to cultivate and study the Buddhadharma together, making Buddhism ever more radiant. Whoever can leave home and cultivate the Way at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas will certainly become a Buddha in the future. Why? Because:

The tower by the water sees the moon first.

(Whoever dwells in the tower beside the lake will see the moon's reflection first.)

If you come to the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas early, you will become a Buddha early.

Whoever comes later will become a Buddha later.

Many people come to the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas but feel they cannot stay, because they find little going on here, the rules too strict, and nothing fun. But you should know: chasing outer pleasures, you will lose true joy. In life, seeking what is false, you lose what is true. To find what is true, you must first let go of what is false and hollow. You cannot both cultivate the world-transcending Way and cling to ordinary worldly dharmas—like stepping into two boats at once, wanting to sail north of the river yet also south. That cannot be done!

In this Buddha-recitation Session, you must "deeply enter through a single door"—focusing on one Dharma-door—relying only on a true, sincere, and reverent heart in practicing Buddha-recitation, without wasting even a minute. Know that a moment of time is a moment of life. Without effort, your offenses only grow. With true effort, your good roots grow. Therefore, sincerely and earnestly recite the Buddha; only then will your time not be wasted, and only then will your life have true worth.

(Explained in winter, 1979, at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas)
